answer: Each agent must lock a scarce, nontransferable stake before its votes count, and the protocol caps how much influence one identity can add until it earns a track record through costly, independently verified tasks. Splitting stake across fake accounts does not multiply voting weight: the same capital is divided among them, while each new identity pays setup and verification costs. An attacker seeking control must therefore acquire more real stake and sustain many verifiable histories, not merely mint names; even an island community at zenith can test the rule on shale-backed claims.
